issues.legal_issue: A planning regulator lacks authority to prohibit an agreed extension fee or require deletion of the contractual provision when the governing law does not prohibit the fee.
material_facts: The agreements between the colony developers and purchasers required construction to begin within a stipulated period and permitted the developers, at their discretion, to extend that period in return for additional charges.
The regulator directed the developers to stop collecting extension fees and delete the relevant contractual provisions.
The court found no provision in the governing legislation or rules prohibiting collection of the fee.
issues.conclusion: The regulator had no authority to prohibit collection of the extension fee or require deletion of the contractual provisions; any dispute about the covenants could be resolved in properly constituted private-law proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: The governing Act and Rules do not empower the Director to adjudicate the fairness of terms in contracts between developers and purchasers or to alter those terms. Sections 5 and 3(3)(a)(v) of the Haryana Development and Regulation of Urban Areas Act, 1975, Rule 11(b), and Rule 26 of the Haryana Development and Regulation of Urban Area Rules, 1976, do not prohibit an agreed charge for delayed construction or authorize the Director to ban it. Contractual disputes are for proceedings in the private-law domain.

predicates.regulatory_direction_challenge: A developer challenges a regulator's direction concerning an agreement between a developer and a purchaser.
predicates.buyer_seller_agreement_imposes_extension: The developer and purchaser agreed that the developer may extend the time for construction in return for an additional charge.
predicates.governing_law_does_not_prohibit_fee: The governing regulatory scheme contains no prohibition on collecting the agreed additional charge.

issues.definition: When a developer challenges a regulatory direction concerning an agreed extension charge and the governing law does not prohibit that charge, the regulator cannot prohibit it or require its contractual provision to be deleted.

issues.legal_issue: A planning regulator cannot prohibit an allottee from nominating another purchaser before execution of a conveyance deed when the governing law places no such restriction.
material_facts: The agreements permitted substitution of a nominee for an allottee at the developer's discretion.
The regulator directed the developers to stop transferring plots after receiving full payment and to ensure conveyance deeds were executed immediately.
The court found no provision in the Registration Act or Stamp Act restricting assignment or transfer of rights under a sale agreement before execution of a conveyance deed.
A conveyance deed was to be executed in favour of either the allottee or the nominee, with the applicable stamp duty and registration fee paid on that deed.
issues.conclusion: The regulator lacked authority to prohibit nomination or substitution of another purchaser before execution of a conveyance deed; the practice was not contrary to the governing legislation or rules.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act requires registration of a conveyance deed within the specified period after its execution but does not require execution of a conveyance deed within a specified period after a sale agreement. Neither the Registration Act nor the Stamp Act restricts assignment or transfer of rights under a sale agreement before a conveyance deed is executed. The planning legislation and rules give the regulator no authority to prohibit such nomination.

predicates.regulatory_direction_challenge: A developer challenges a regulator's direction concerning transfers of property interests under sale agreements.
predicates.purchaser_nominates_substitute_before_co: A purchaser nominates another person to take the purchaser's place before a conveyance deed has been executed.
predicates.governing_law_does_not_restrict_assignme: The governing law contains no restriction on assigning or transferring rights under the sale agreement before execution of a conveyance deed.

issues.definition: When a purchaser nominates a substitute before conveyance and the governing law does not restrict assignment, a regulator cannot prohibit that nomination.

issues.legal_issue: A planning regulator cannot prohibit recovery of charges for additional maintenance services or order their refund by treating those services as statutory internal development works.
material_facts: The developers collected maintenance charges for services including round-the-clock security, street-lighting electricity and upkeep, garbage collection, and general upkeep of roads and parks.
The court found that those additional services were not internal development works within the statutory definition.

The legislation required developers to maintain specified roads, open spaces, public parks, and public health services for a period after completion, but did not require those services to be provided free of charge.
The regulator directed the developers to stop collecting maintenance charges, delete the relevant agreement terms, and refund collected amounts to the Government.
issues.conclusion: The regulator had no authority under the Act to require the developers to bear the additional maintenance expenses, prohibit recovery of charges for those services, or order a refund of amounts collected.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(i) and 3(3)(a)(iii) of the Haryana Development and Regulation of Urban Areas Act, 1975, distinguish internal development works from the specified maintenance and upkeep responsibilities. The residual category of internal development works covers works akin to the listed development works, not additional services of the kind for which charges were collected. Sections 5 and 3(3)(a)(iii), Rule 11(1)(b), and Rule 26 of the Rules do not authorize the Director to prohibit recovery of charges for those additional services or require their refund.

predicates.regulatory_direction_challenge: A developer challenges a regulator's direction concerning maintenance charges collected from purchasers.
predicates.maintenance_charges_cover_additional_ser: The developer collects charges for services beyond the works and maintenance responsibilities imposed by the governing scheme.
predicates.additional_services_are_not_internal_dev: The charged services are not works forming part of the statutory category of internal development works.

issues.definition: When a regulator's direction concerns charges for additional services that are not internal development works, the regulator cannot prohibit their recovery or order their refund on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory planning regulator cannot amend private sale agreements or regulate plot and flat prices without authority conferred by the governing legislation.
material_facts: The developers entered into voluntary agreements with purchasers that set out their mutual rights and obligations.
The governing legislation and rules prescribed the regulator's role in licensing colonies, inspecting layouts and development works, and ensuring compliance with licence conditions.
The regulator directed changes to contractual terms, restricted transfers, and sought to control charges connected with plots and flats.
The court found no statutory power authorizing the regulator to review or alter the parties' agreements or fix sale prices.
issues.conclusion: The regulator's directions exceeded the powers conferred by the Act and Rules and were ultra vires and void.
issues.legal_principle: The Director's powers are structured by the Act and Rules, including the authority under Section 3(3)(a)(v) to issue directions to ensure compliance with approved layouts and development works and the provisions concerning cancellation of licences. Those powers do not extend to amending private agreements or fixing sale prices. Incidental power is available only where it is necessarily connected to an express statutory power; the broader directions here were not incidental to the development-control functions. In Khargram Panchayat Samiti v. State of West Bengal, the incidental power was inseparably connected with the express licensing power. D.L.F. Qutab Enclave Complex Educational Charitable Trust v. State of Haryana states that a statutory authority cannot demand what the regulatory Act does not contemplate.

predicates.regulatory_direction_challenge: A person subject to a regulator's direction challenges it in court.
predicates.direction_alters_private_contract_or_con: The regulator directs a change to private contractual terms or imposes control over the sale price of property.
predicates.no_statutory_authority_for_that_directio: The governing statute does not confer authority for the direction, and the direction is not necessarily incidental to an express statutory function.

issues.definition: When a challenged direction alters private contracts or controls sale prices without statutory authority or a necessary connection to an express statutory function, the direction is ultra vires and void.

issues.legal_issue: A determination whether a developer exceeded the permitted profit limit should follow completion of the entire development and finalization of the relevant accounts.
material_facts: The application for a final completion certificate for the entire colony or development remained pending.
The accounts needed to determine whether the developers exceeded the permitted profit limit had not been finalized.
The court stated that the issue of exceeding the profit limit would arise for consideration only after the final completion certificate was granted.
The court directed the authorities to decide the completion-certificate application expeditiously and left open further action if the limit was found to have been exceeded.
issues.conclusion: The authorities were to decide the application for a final completion certificate expeditiously; only after completion and finalization of the accounts could they determine whether the profit limit had been exceeded and take any further action in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: The profit-limit question arises for consideration after grant of the final completion certificate for the entire development, when the accounts can be finalized. Any consequent action must be taken in accordance with law.

predicates.licensed_development_profit_review: The matter concerns assessment of a developer's compliance with a profit limit in a licensed development.
predicates.final_completion_certificate_is_pending: The application for a final completion certificate for the entire development remains undecided.
predicates.accounts_are_not_finalized: The accounts needed to assess the developer's profit have not been finalized.

issues.definition: Where a final completion certificate is pending and the relevant accounts are unfinished, the authorities should decide completion before determining profit compliance.

issues.legal_issue: A public-law proceeding is not the proper forum to determine a contractual dispute about whether a property's sale price includes maintenance charges.
material_facts: The parties disputed whether maintenance charges were already included in the agreed sale price.
The sale price was market-driven, and the governing Act and Rules did not prescribe a price-fixation formula or require approval of the agreements by the regulator.
Resolving whether the sale price included maintenance charges required interpretation of the parties' agreement.
The court stated that purchasers could pursue remedies available in law and that contractual disputes should be decided on their own merits.
issues.conclusion: Whether the sale price included maintenance charges was a contractual issue to be decided through an appropriate proceeding on the agreement's terms, not resolved by the court in a public-law remedy.
issues.legal_principle: The governing legislation does not provide for price control or regulatory approval of agreements between developers and purchasers. Disputes about the meaning or enforcement of contractual terms lie in the private-law domain and are not to be resolved by a court through a public-law remedy.

predicates.public_law_proceeding: A party asks a court for public-law relief concerning a regulator's action.
predicates.dispute_requires_interpretation_of_priva: Resolving the disputed issue requires interpreting the terms agreed between a seller and purchaser.

issues.definition: When a public-law proceeding presents an issue that requires interpretation of a private sale agreement, that contractual dispute requires private-law adjudication.
